questions.stem: An 82-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of fever and confusion. He had a history of atrial fibrillation, CABG 4 years ago, benign prostatic hypertrophy, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He was a resident in a nursing home and had a long-term catheter in situ. He had been treated presumptively for a urinary tract infection but had deteriorated. On examination his GCS was 13/15, his temperature was 38.1°C, and his heart rate was 112 beats/minute. His blood pressure was 128/68 mmHg. It was not possible to formally examine his neurologic systems, but his reflexes were universally brisk and his tone increased. There were no lateralizing signs. Pupils were equal and reactive to light. He was admitted and treated with antibiotics for presumed urosepsis. Two days after his admission, he had a tonic clonic seizure on the ward. An urgent MRI showed temporal lobe enhancement, and a lumbar puncture showed a lymphocytic CSF with a raised red cell count. CSF PCR was positive for HSV-1. Six months after discharge he was still suffering from significant cognitive impairment with behavioral abnormalities.
questions.lead_in: What factor in this case is associated with a poor outcome?

options.text: MRI changes in the temporal lobes

questions.explanation: Delay in initiating aciclovir therapy Herpes encephalitis carries a high morbidity and mortality even with prompt diagnosis and appropriate treatment. A multivariate analysis identified two factors associated with a poorer outcome. These were a high “simplified acute physiology score” at admission and a delay of longer than 2 days between admission and starting aciclovir therapy.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q11

questions.question: Young patient with long vignette of asymptomatic bacteriuria on post appendectomy? Foley cath. His urine is cloudy and nauseating. A culture is positive for E. coli and the antibiogram is given. What is the management?

cohort_answer.text: No treatment. Change foley cath. Monitor clinically

questions.question: A woman in hospital with cloudy foul smelling urine with indwelling foley. T 37.2C, WBC 12, post-op appendectomy. Otherwise no symptoms. Growing something that's pretty sensitive in Ucx, some leuks on UA.

cohort_answer.text: Remove Foley. No abx indicated. IDSA: in patients with short-term indwelling urethral catheter (<30 days), recommend against screening for or treating asymptomatic bacteriuria (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence)

questions.question: You are seeing a patient with a catheter-associated UTI.

parts.text: What factor is the MOST important factor associated with catheter associated UTI?
What THREE options could be used instead of an indwelling urethral catheter in a patient requiring a catheter?
In a male patient with uncomplicated febrile catheter associated UTI, what would be the typical treatment duration?

questions.model_answer: a) Most important risk factor: duration of urinary catheterization. b) Three alternatives to an indwelling urethral catheter: condom (external) catheter, intermittent catheterization, and suprapubic catheterization. c) Typical treatment duration for uncomplicated febrile CAUTI in a male with prompt clinical response: 7 days (extending to 10-14 days if response to therapy is delayed).
questions.cites: Mandell pp. 3588-3589, 3594 (CAUTI risk factors, alternatives to indwelling catheters, IDSA-based treatment duration)
